title: The two-minute drill: 64 yards in 34 seconds with no timeouts (Commanders vs. Bengals)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run. It still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, no snaps logged) and no review files. The original football-film-room repo could not be read from this run (GitHub access for it isn't enabled for this scheduled task). So there are no new misses to target. This lesson adds a new situation concept, built on Lesson 63 (pressure) and the end-of-game calls you'll see all Thanksgiving week, using Monday night's finish.

The big idea: the "two-minute drill" is how an offense moves fast when time is short.Every play is a race against the clock. The offense wants yards and a stopped clock.Monday, Washington needed a field goal with 39 seconds left, no timeouts, starting at its own 28.

  1. A · The start. Own 28, 39 seconds, no timeouts. A field goal wins it.Field-goal range in the NFL starts around the opponent's 35 (a 52-yard try). So Washington needed about 37 yards.
  2. B · First throw: 22 yards to Antonio Williams. He was tackled in bounds, so the clock kept running.With no timeouts, the offense has to sprint to the line and snap again.
  3. C · Second throw: 42 yards to Williams, to the Cincinnati 8. Now they're deep in range, but the clock is still moving.
  4. D · The spike. Jayden Daniels threw the ball straight into the ground. That counts as an incomplete pass.It costs a down, but it stops the clock. It stopped with 5 seconds left.
  5. E · The kick. Drew Stevens made a 26-yard field goal as time expired: Commanders 22, Bengals 20.The whole drive took 34 seconds.

Why the Bengals lost the clock battle: their 56-yard field goal (Evan McPherson) put them ahead 20-19 with 46 seconds left.Scoring fast left Washington time. A drive that burned the clock first would have left less.Earlier, Washington coach Dan Quinn kicked a field goal on 4th-and-1 with 2:26 left instead of going for it. ESPN called it questionable. It gave Cincinnati the ball back with time to answer.

College is different: in college football the clock stops briefly after every first down until the ball is set.That gives college offenses extra time. It's one reason late college comebacks happen more, like Rutgers scoring the winning TD and 2-point try as time expired against Penn State Saturday.

Why it matters for bets: late field goals swing totals and passing yards.Monday's last 2:26 had three field goals (9 points). Burrow's 300 needed his late throws too.If you hold an Under, a close game in the last two minutes is a danger zone. If you hold a QB Over, it's a friend.

For your Film Room drill: in a two-minute drill, log "pass" almost every snap. Watch for the hurry-up: no huddle, receivers running to the sideline.A run usually means the offense has a timeout left, or it's killing the clock with the lead.

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 6: Situations)

o: Stops the clock and costs a down
quiz.w: Throwing the ball into the ground counts as an incomplete pass: the clock stops, and the offense uses up a down.

quiz.q: In the NFL, a receiver catches a pass and is tackled in bounds with 30 seconds left. The offense has no timeouts. What happens to the clock?
o: It stops until the next snap
quiz.w: A catch in bounds keeps the clock running. That's why Washington had to hurry and spike.

quiz.q: What's one clock rule that helps college two-minute drills more than NFL ones?
o: The college clock stops briefly after every first down
quiz.w: In college the clock stops after a first down until the ball is set, which saves offenses time.

quiz.q: Before the snap, the offense is in a no-huddle hurry-up with 40 seconds left and no timeouts, down 2. What should you log?
quiz.w: Down with little time and no timeouts, the offense almost always throws, often toward the sideline.
